overview.title: 📖 Overview: From Animal Blemishes to Priestly Ones
overview.subtitle: Bekhorot 43a–43b
overview.hebrewSource: מוּמִין אֵלּוּ, בֵּין קְבוּעִין בֵּין עוֹבְרִים — פּוֹסְלִין בָּאָדָם, וְיָתֵר עֲלֵיהֶן
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: After a final note closing the tumtum discussion, the mishna opens a new chapter: every blemish that disqualifies an animal from the altar also disqualifies a priest from Temple service — and priests have additional disqualifying blemishes all their own, since a priest must simply look 'equal to the seed of Aaron.' The Gemara derives the overlap between human and animal blemish lists through a verbal analogy on 'garav' and 'yalefet,' then explains why the Torah needed to write the law of disqualifying blemishes three separate times — for a person, for sacrificial animals, and for a firstborn. The daf catalogues an array of head-shape and baldness blemishes unique to priests, then opens two new mishnayot defining the eyebrow blemish (gibben) and the nose blemish (ḥarum).

slides.title: 👰 Closing the Tumtum Sugya
slides.hebrewSource: לִפְסוֹל בִּמְקוֹם אַחִים... וְלַחְלוֹץ שֶׁלֹּא בִּמְקוֹם אַחִים, אִיכָּא בֵּינַיְיהוּ
slides.label: The practical difference:
slides.text: Between Rabbi Yehuda (who treats a human tumtum as a certain eunuch) and Rabbi Yosei b'Rabbi Yehuda (who treats him as merely uncertain): if the deceased brother had other brothers, Rabbi Yehuda's view frees the widow to marry any of them without the tumtum's ḥalitza, since his ḥalitza means nothing; Rabbi Yosei's view requires it, since the tumtum might genuinely be a valid male whose ḥalitza would otherwise leave her improperly released. And if the tumtum is the ONLY brother, Rabbi Yehuda exempts her from ḥalitza entirely, while Rabbi Yosei still requires it, just in case.

slides.title: 🔗 New Chapter: Linking Human and Animal Blemishes
slides.subtitle: A verbal analogy imports each list's unique terms into the other

lines.speaker: Gemara
lines.text: Why does the mishna say all of an animal's disqualifying blemishes disqualify a priest too? A wart (yabelet) is written only regarding animals; a cataract (dak) and tevallul are written only regarding people!

lines.speaker: Resolution
lines.text: They're derived from each other: the word גָּרָב ('garav') appears in both lists, and so does יַלֶּפֶת ('yalefet') — a verbal analogy (גְּזֵירָה שָׁוָה) transfers each list's unique blemishes to the other.

lines.speaker: Gemara
lines.text: But is this analogy even valid, or could logic refute it — an animal is stricter since IT is sacrificed; a person is stricter since he's obligated in mitzvot?

lines.speaker: Resolution
lines.text: The terms are 'free' (superfluous) in context — since if scurvy alone sufficed to prove repulsive garav a fortiori, why repeat garav explicitly? Being free, the analogy stands unchallenged by logic.

callout.label: Why not write it all just once?
callout.text: The school of Rabbi Yishmael: every repeated passage teaches something new — here, the blemishes unique to each side (hooves/gums for animals; hunched back/sunken nose for people).

slides.title: 📜 Rava's Three Necessary Verses
slides.subtitle: Why 'blemish disqualifies' had to be written separately for a person, sacrifices, and a firstborn
headers: Can't be derived from the other two because...
rows: He is uniquely obligated in mitzvot generally — unlike an animal
They are themselves offered on the altar, and consecration is voluntary — sanctity applies to many types
Its sanctity begins automatically from birth (from the womb), unlike animals consecrated by a person's choice

callout.label: Each pairing tested and rejected:
callout.text: The Gemara systematically shows no single case's blemish-disqualification can be logically inferred even from the OTHER TWO combined — each has some unique stringency the others lack.

slides.title: 👨 Head-Shapes and Baldness That Disqualify a Priest
slides.subtitle: Blemishes unique to a person, since a priest must look 'equal to the seed of Aaron'

boxes.title: Head Shapes
items: Kilon: pointed, narrow above/wide below (like a barrel lid)
Shakut/Sekifat: indented forehead / protruding back of head

boxes.title: Back and Baldness
items: Hunched back WITH a bone: disqualified by all
Hunched back with only flesh: disputed (R' Yehuda: fit; Rabbis: not equal to Aaron's seed)
Kere'ach (bald): disqualified only if missing hair specifically at the BACK of the head (Rava)

callout.label: Rabbi Yoḥanan's addition:
callout.text: Bald priests, dwarves, and those with 'leaky eyes' are disqualified by TORAH law (not equal to Aaron's seed) — against a baraita (Rabbi Yehuda's view) that would include bald priests via 'the priests' (הַכֹּהֲנִים) in Leviticus 1:8.

slides.title: 👁️ New Mishnayot: Gibben (Eyebrows) and Ḥarum (Nose)
slides.subtitle: Torah terms defined — and disputed
rows: No eyebrows, or only one eyebrow
R' Dosa: eyebrows so long they lie flat and cover the eyes; R' Ḥanina b. Antigonus: a crooked spine appearing as two backs
Sunken nose (can paint both eyes as one brushstroke)
Also includes: retreating, blocked, or drooping nose ('or ḥarum' includes all); Rabbi Yosei's narrower view was rejected as 'going too far'

callout.label: A near-fatal clarification:
callout.text: When Rav Shimi bar Ḥiyya challenged that 'two spines' should mean the person couldn't even survive, Rav clarified: it means a crooked spine only APPEARING doubled — a livable, disqualifying condition, not literally two spines.

summary.principle: A new chapter establishes that every blemish disqualifying an animal also disqualifies a priest, links the two lists through a verbal analogy on 'garav' and 'yalefet,' and catalogues an extensive array of head, back, eyebrow, and nose conditions unique to a priest — all rooted in the requirement that he look 'equal to the seed of Aaron.'

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: a priest must look 'equal to the seed of Aaron' — a standard broader than, and linked to, the physical blemishes that disqualify sacrificial animals

quiz.q: What is the practical difference between Rabbi Yehuda's and Rabbi Yosei b'Rabbi Yehuda's views on a human tumtum's levirate marriage status?
o: There is no practical difference
Rabbi Yehuda treats him as a certain eunuch (so his ḥalitza is meaningless), while Rabbi Yosei treats him as uncertain (so his ḥalitza is still required, just in case)
Both agree completely on all cases
Only Rabbi Yosei allows levirate marriage at all
quiz.e: Since Rabbi Yehuda considers the tumtum a definite eunuch, his ḥalitza has no legal effect; Rabbi Yosei's view that the tumtum might be a valid male means his ḥalitza is still necessary to properly release the widow.

quiz.q: How does the Gemara derive that animal blemishes like a wart (yabelet) also disqualify a priest, even though the Torah doesn't explicitly write 'wart' regarding a person?
o: By simple logical inference with no verse needed
Through a verbal analogy (gezeira shava) using the shared terms 'garav' and 'yalefet,' which appear in both the human and animal blemish lists
It is not derived at all; the mishna's ruling is rejected
By counting the total number of blemishes in each list
quiz.e: The Gemara identifies the words garav and yalefet as appearing in both contexts, establishing a verbal analogy that transfers each list's unique blemishes to the other.

quiz.q: According to Rava, why couldn't the Torah's rule that blemishes disqualify a firstborn be derived from the parallel rules for a person and for sacrificial animals combined?
o: Because a firstborn cannot have blemishes at all

Because both a person and sacrificial animals have a stringency a firstborn lacks — a person is obligated in many mitzvot, and other offerings encompass many types with voluntary consecration, while a firstborn's sanctity is singular and automatic from birth
Because firstborns are never actually sacrificed
Because the three cases are entirely unrelated
quiz.e: Rava shows that each of the three categories (person, sacrifices, firstborn) has some unique stringency not shared by the other two, so none can be fully derived from the others, requiring all three verses.

quiz.q: According to Rava's ruling on baldness (kere'ach), when is a priest disqualified from Temple service?
o: Whenever he has any hair loss anywhere
Specifically when he lacks a row of hair at the BACK of his head (even if he has hair in front)
Only if he is completely bald all over
Baldness never disqualifies a priest
quiz.e: Rava clarifies that the disqualifying condition is lacking hair specifically at the back of the head; having hair only in the back but not the front is actually considered fit, as is typical for older men.

quiz.q: According to the mishna and the Gemara's clarification, what does Rabbi Ḥanina ben Antigonus mean by a gibben having 'two backs and two spines'?
o: A person literally born with two separate spines
A person whose spine is crooked, making it appear as though there are two spines, though he can survive normally
A fictional condition that doesn't exist
Someone with an extra vertebra only
quiz.e: Rav clarified to his grandson that this refers to a crooked spine that merely appears doubled, not a literal second spine, which would be incompatible with survival.
